newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Slower Czech growth highlights need for change.
newsitem.headline: Slower Czech growth highlights need for change.

text.p: Data released this week show Czech economic growth slowing more quickly than expected and have further highlighted the need for restructuring to tackle fundamental problems, economists said on Friday.

The Czech Statistical Bureau (CSU) said on Wednesday that real industrial output contracted by 3.9 percent year on year in January and that construction output was 18.6 percent lower than a year earlier. At the same time, average industrial wages grew 14.4 percent in nominal terms.
"Suddenly it seems that there are more clouds over the economy and, to be honest, nobody expected that," said Patria Finance economist Vladimir Kreidl.
"The construction output and industrial output figures for January were unexpectedly bad," he said, adding that this could have an impact on 1997 GDP growth expectations.

The Czech economy has enjoyed seven years of demand-led growth as industry imported technology and the population, which has seen its wages rise sharply over the past few years, slaked its thirst for consumer goods.

However, some economists say industrial output has failed to keep pace with wages, and in fact weakened recently, indicating that investment has not been effective and that industry has not carried out vital restructuring.
Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus, in a speech to business leaders on Tuesday, said 1996 gross domestic product growth ended the year one percent lower than expected.
He revised downards his forecast for 1997 GDP growth to more than four percent and blamed the slower growth on an over-restrictive anti-inflation stance at the central bank.
Fourth quarter and full-year 1996 figures are expected next Friday and Kreidl said Patria forecast both at four percent. GDP growth in 1997 was also seen at four percent.
Klaus said on Tuesday he expected GDP growth in 1997 of higher than four percent, adding this was a "very fitting result" in a European context.
However, this was a marked downward revision from the 5.4 percent growth forecast on which the 1997 budget was based.
"On the one hand you see some negative news from the economy and on the other you see politicians surprised by those developments and trying to find solutions," said Kreidl.
Zivnostenska Banka chief economist Pavel Sobisek also said he believed fourth quarter 1996 GDP growth would be lower than forecast and could be as low as three percent.
"If something doesn't change significantly, I can imagine that growth would further slow down and that the economy would get into recession," he said.
Klaus said the economy's main problem was the trade deficit, which widened to 160.3 billion crowns ($5.5 billion) last year.
He said devaluation of the crown, which strengthened significantly earlier this year, was not the right solution.

IPB Banka chief economist Miroslav Soucek said the fall in industrial output reflected poor export performance but added that a devaluation would solve nothing as higher import prices would hit Czech exports of intermediate goods.
Economists also warned against looser monetary policy.

"The slowdown in money supply was inevitable. It was the right step and not the main negative influence on the economy. I would blame rather more general problems like corprorate governance and the state of the capital markets," said Sobisek.
Kreidl said the trade gap would drive the 1996 current account deficit to 8.5 percent of GDP in 1996 from about four percent in 1995.
"It is natural for a country in such a state of development as the Czech Republic to have a current account deficit and to finance it fom foreign investment.
"The problem is the scope of the deficit and that is something where we have exceeded all safe limits," he said. ($ = 29.03 Czech Crowns)
